claim: Deep learning-based methods have advanced animal pose estimation, enhancing accuracy and efficiency in quantifying animal behavior.
source: Deep learning-based methods have advanced animal pose estimation, enhancing accuracy, and efficiency in quantifying animal behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript.

claim: Deep learning-based methods frequently experience tracking drift, where noise-induced jumps in body point estimates compromise reliability.
source: However, these methods frequently experience tracking drift, where noise-induced jumps in body point estimates compromise reliability.
evidence: This is stated as a known problem in the field, supported by the manuscript's motivation and references to existing literature.

claim: ADPT significantly reduces drift and surpasses existing models like DeepLabCut and SLEAP in accuracy across cross-species datasets.
source: Extensive experiments across cross-species datasets—including proprietary mouse and monkey recordings and public Drosophila and macaque datasets—demonstrate that ADPT significantly reduces drift and surpasses existing models like DeepLabCut and SLEAP in accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results presented throughout the manuscript, including Figures 2-5.

claim: ADPT achieved 93.16% identification accuracy for 10 unmarked mice.
source: Moreover, ADPT achieved 93.16% identification accuracy for 10 unmarked mice and 90.36% accuracy for freely interacting unmarked mice, which can be further refined to 99.72%, enhancing both anti-drift performance and pose estimation accuracy in social interactions.
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from experiments described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ADPT achieved 90.36% accuracy for freely interacting unmarked mice, which can be further refined to 99.72%.
source: Moreover, ADPT achieved 93.16% identification accuracy for 10 unmarked mice and 90.36% accuracy for freely interacting unmarked mice, which can be further refined to 99.72%, enhancing both anti-drift performance and pose estimation accuracy in social interactions.
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from experiments described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: ADPT is computationally efficient and suitable for real-time analysis with its end-to-end design.
source: With its end-to-end design, ADPT is computationally efficient and suitable for real-time analysis, offering a robust solution for reproducible animal behavior studies.
evidence: This is supported by inference speed measurements reported in the manuscript showing 90±4 fps.

claim: Animal behavior is shaped by environment, genetics, diseases, cognitive states, and social interactions.
source: Animal behavior is a complex and dynamic phenomenon that is shaped by a wide range of factors, including environment, genetics, diseases, cognitive states, and social interactions (Robinson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robinson et al., 2008.

claim: Understanding the underlying mechanisms and neural correlates of animal behaviors requires accurate and detailed pose tracking.
source: Understanding the underlying mechanisms and neural correlates of animal behaviors requires accurate and detailed pose tracking as they move freely (Pereira et al., 2020; Krakauer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pereira et al., 2020 and Krakauer et al., 2017.

claim: Deep learning-based tools such as DeepLabCut, SLEAP, and DeepPoseKit offer the feasibility of automatically quantifying complex freely moving animal behaviors from videos.
source: Recently, deep learning-based tools such as DeepLabCut, SLEAP, and DeepPoseKit have offered the feasibility of automatically quantifying complex freely moving animal behaviors from videos recorded by contactless cameras (Mathis et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2022; Graving et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the respective tool publications.

claim: Deep learning methods are susceptible to uncertainty and noise interference, leading to tracking drift.
source: Nevertheless, these deep learning methods are susceptible to uncertainty and noise interference, leading to tracking drift due to errors in the detection of one or more keypoints, in the estimated keypoint dynamics (Weinreb et al., 2024; Hsu and Yttri, 2021; Lonini et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Weinreb et al., 2024; Hsu and Yttri, 2021; Lonini et al., 2022.

claim: Drift in keypoints estimates can affect subsequent animal behavior statistics and downstream tasks such as behavior classification, individual identification, and social behavior clustering.
source: Such drift in keypoints estimates can broadly affect subsequent animal behavior statistics and downstream tasks, such as behavior classification, individual identification, and social behavior clustering (Sheppard et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sheppard et al., 2022 and Huang et al., 2021.

claim: Tracking drift severely jeopardizes the reliability and repeatability of ethological studies.
source: It severely jeopardizes the reliability and repeatability of ethological studies.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the described impacts of tracking drift on downstream analyses.

claim: Animal gait analysis relies on accurate tracking of limbs and paws.
source: For example, animal gait analysis relies on accurate tracking of limbs and paws (Sheppard et al., 2022), and behavioral classification relies on the dynamics of body keypoints (Huang et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sheppard et al., 2022.

claim: Behavioral classification relies on the dynamics of body keypoints.
source: For example, animal gait analysis relies on accurate tracking of limbs and paws (Sheppard et al., 2022), and behavioral classification relies on the dynamics of body keypoints (Huang et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2021 and Han et al., 2022.

claim: Deep learning pose estimation has not achieved the reliability of classical kinematic analysis.
source: So far, deep learning pose estimation has not achieved the reliability of classical kinematic analysis, which often involves post-processing in real-world applications (Niknejad et al., 2023; Aljovic et al., 2022; Weinreb et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Niknejad et al., 2023; Aljovic et al., 2022; Weinreb et al., 2024.

claim: Drifted keypoints may be unsystematically distributed within each predefined behavior class, misleading the decision boundaries of the behavior class.
source: The drifted keypoints may be unsystematically distributed within each predefined behavior class, misleading the decision boundaries of the behavior class, thereby reducing the performance of supervised behavior classification Gabriel et al., 2022 or unsupervised behavior representation (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gabriel et al., 2022 and Huang et al., 2021.

claim: State-of-the-art deep learning methods such as DeepLabCut and SLEAP have no effective strategies to avoid tracking drift.
source: Even the state-of-the-art (SOTA) deep learning methods such as DeepLabCut and SLEAP have no effective strategies to avoid the tracking drift (Weinreb et al., 2024; Mathis et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2022; Graving et al., 2019; Lauer et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple papers including Weinreb et al., 2024; Mathis et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2022; Graving et al., 2019; Lauer et al., 2022.

claim: DeepLabCut and SLEAP both embed a user interface to allow humans to exclude and rectify outliers frame by frame.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mathis et al., 2018 and Pereira et al., 2022.

claim: Human refinement restricts the efficiency of biological experiments when facing millions of drifted frames.
source: Although it would be the golden criterion to reduce the tracking drift, this strategy restricts the efficiency of the biological experiment when the human faces millions of drifted frames.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the practical limitations of manual correction.

claim: Signal processing filters such as median filter and low pass filter can efficiently remove most drifted points without human intervention.
source: The second strategy is signal processing filters such as median filter and low pass filter (Stenum et al., 2021; Pereira et al., 2019; Luxem et al., 2022; Weinreb et al., 2024; Han et al., 2024; Li and Lee, 2021). They can efficiently remove most of the drifted points without human intervention, but they will also remove the subtle behaviors with high-frequency features such as self-grooming in autism mouse models (Huang et al., 2021) or tremor in animal models of Parkinson's disease (Baker et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple papers on filtering methods.

claim: Signal processing filters will also remove subtle behaviors with high-frequency features such as self-grooming in autism mouse models or tremor in animal models of Parkinson's disease.
source: The second strategy is signal processing filters such as median filter and low pass filter (Stenum et al., 2021; Pereira et al., 2019; Luxem et al., 2022; Weinreb et al., 2024; Han et al., 2024; Li and Lee, 2021). evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2021 and Baker et al., 2022.

claim: Linear dynamic models such as Keypoint-Moseq and adaptive Kalman filter can reduce drift and maintain high-frequency behaviors at the same time.
source: The third strategy is fitting the drifted frames using linear dynamic models such as Keypoint-Moseq (Weinreb et al., 2024) and adaptive Kalman filter (Huang et al., 2022). They can reduce the drift and maintain the high-frequency behaviors at the same time.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Weinreb et al., 2024 and Huang et al., 2022.

claim: The performance of linear dynamic models drops sharply when processing continuous and long-duration drifted frames.
source: Nevertheless, the performance of these models would drop sharply when processing continuous and long-duration drifted frames.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods based on the authors' understanding of the field.

claim: DeepLabCut, SLEAP, and DeepPoseKit all take the convolutional neural network (CNN) as the main component of pose estimation ANNs, which is the core problem causing tracking drift.
source: DeepLabCut, SLEAP, and DeepPoseKit all take the convolutional neural network (CNN) as the main component of pose estimation ANNs, which is the core problem causing tracking drift (Mathis et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2022; Graving et al., 2019; Lauer et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim combines factual information about the architectures (supported by citations) with an inference about the cause of tracking drift.

claim: The limited working memory of the CNN makes it easy to be influenced by content-independent parameters to predict wrong locations of keypoints.
source: The limited working memory of the CNN makes it easy to be influenced by the content-independent parameters to predict the wrong locations of keypoints and finally cause tracking drift (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2021.

claim: The Transformer is more efficient to capture global dependent features of images than CNN.
source: To avoid this drawback, the Transformer becomes a better option to construct pose estimation ANNs because it is more efficient to capture global dependent features of images (Yang et al., 2021; Stoffl et al., 2021; Xu and Zhang, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2021; Stoffl et al., 2021; Xu and Zhang, 2022.
